twitter.content: Section 122 expires at 12:01 am on 24 July 2026 absent Congressional extension — this is a statutory cliff, not a political choice. Tariffs are taxes paid by US importers and ultimately consumers. Article I authority over tariffs belongs to Congress, and the House tariff-rebellion caucus will not rubber-stamp a multi-trillion-dollar revenue extension without offsets, sunset clauses, and a reciprocal-process mandate. The administration's parallel Section 301 buildout is the tell: they are planning around the lapse, not fighting for extension. We will insist on a transparent review mechanism and a hard sunset before any extension is considered.

Post-SCOTUS, tariffs will 'snap back to exactly where they were' via Section 232 sectoral actions, Section 301 country-by-country investigations, and Section 122 as a bridge instrument. The IEEPA ruling closed one door; it did not close the President's statutory trade authorities. We expect the effective tariff rate to stabilize in the 7-12% range through 2028, with Section 232 on semiconductors (25% on high-end AI chips) and pharmaceuticals (100% with UK carve-out at 10%) anchoring the floor. Treasury is managing the $166-175B IEEPA refund pool without fiscal disorder; TGA build-up is on track.

USTR has completed findings on 60 Section 301 forced-labor investigations as of 2 June 2026: 12.5% ad valorem duties on 46 trading partners, 10% on 14 others. This is the durable substitute for the IEEPA reciprocal-tariff regime. Combined with surviving Section 301 China actions (Lists 1-3 at 25%, List 4A at 7.5%), the buildout is legally resilient under existing statute and consistent with the post-SCOTUS major-questions doctrine. We are also operating USMCA on annual joint reviews rather than a 16-year renewal — predictable, conditional, and enforceable.

Section 232 is the legal backbone of the post-IEEPA tariff regime. We have imposed 50% on high-metal-content steel, 25% on derivatives with a 15% floor, 25% on high-end AI chips since January 2026, and 100% on patented pharmaceuticals effective April 2026 with a 10% UK carve-out. Investigations on lumber and critical minerals are pending. These actions rest on national-security findings that have survived every court challenge since the 1980s. Combined with the CHIPS Program Office's $52.7B direct disbursement pipeline and Coherent's $50M Indiana LOI, we are constructing a coherent industrial-policy portfolio across chips, pharma, and AI.

The Court's 6-3 ruling in Learning Resources v. Trump rests on a clear principle: 'IEEPA contains no reference to tariffs or duties.' Tariffs are taxes, and taxes require clear congressional authorization under the major-questions doctrine. This does not invalidate Sections 232, 301, or 122 — statutes that expressly contemplate tariff action — but it does cabin the President's claimed authority under emergency-economics statutes. Future executive tariff claims will be measured against the clarity of delegation Congress actually provided.

BIS closed the Blackwell loophole on 31 May 2026 and extended the Approved IC Designer licensing accommodation to 31 December 2026. Export controls must be calibrated to deny the PRC access to advanced compute while preserving commercial channels for vetted partners — including the November 2025 approvals of 35,000 Nvidia GB300 equivalents each to UAE G42 and Saudi Humain. The 50% Section 232 tariff on high-end AI chips since January 2026 reinforces the licensing regime. We are tightening the pipe without breaking it.

The CHIPS Program Office is committed to a $52.7B direct-disbursement pipeline under the CHIPS and Science Act. TSMC Arizona remains the lead Tier-1 recipient, with 2nm localization proceeding under Taiwan MOEA clearance. We are aware of reported NIST restructuring and inter-agency pressures; disbursement timelines for Samsung, Intel, and Micron remain on schedule, and the 16 June 2026 LOI with Coherent for up to $50M in Indiana illustrates that downstream applications are also being anchored domestically. The Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit (AMIC) extension vote before 31 December 2026 is the next fiscal cliff.

TSMC's Arizona Fab 21 Phase 2/3 — 2nm and sub-2nm nodes — is on track subject to Taiwan MOEA's gating approval for outbound process-technology transfer. We are the sole source of ≤2nm fabrication at scale and recognize that the US disbursement pipeline is conditional on localization milestones. The Federal Circuit merits review of Section 232 and any CHIPS-program restructuring under NIST are open variables, but our capex envelope through 2028 is committed.

USMCA was not renewed on 1 July 2026. We are operating the agreement under annual joint reviews, beginning with Round 3 the week of 20 July 2026, and the USITC auto rules-of-origin report due 2027 will frame the next negotiation. Canada and Mexico prefer status quo; the United States prefers conditional, enforceable review. This framework preserves USMCA market access while creating leverage on labor-value-content, auto-RoO, and non-market-practices chapters. Withdrawal remains a tail risk; managed review is the base case.

At MC14 Yaoundé in March 2026, DG Okonjo-Iweala framed the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA) as a 'bridge' for appellate review while broader WTO reform proceeds. The United States has vetoed Appellate Body appointments continuously since December 2019. The MPIA now covers 57 members; the EU, China, and Canada are active participants. Absent a US re-engagement, the de facto WTO appellate architecture for trade-restraint disputes will operate outside US participation through 2028.

The Federal Reserve will not bail out fiscal tariff policy. Tariff-driven inflation contributed roughly +0.8 percentage points to core PCE over the last year. I will hold the policy rate at 3.50-3.75% as long as 2% inflation expectations remain unanchored. Productivity gains from AI capex — hyperscalers are spending ~$700-830B in 2026 with 75% directed at AI workloads — are a supply-side offset, but they are not yet large enough to neutralize the tariff impulse. The Committee is data-dependent and tariff-aware.

The USMCA annual-review track, the UK pharmaceutical arrangement, and any forthcoming bilateral outcomes will function more reliably when the multilateral floor beneath them is intact. A bilateral arrangement built atop a fragmented global architecture inherits that fragmentation. Predictability for American exporters, importers, and consumers is itself a function of the multilateral backstop USTR declines to re-engage with.

A predictable trading order serves every nation's interest, including America's.

Third, China honors the Busan consensus and will continue to do so. The PRC administers export controls over gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials in accordance with law and international obligations. We participate actively in the MPIA. We support MC14 reform of the broader WTO architecture. We purchase soybeans at scale and on schedule. These are not concessions. They are the responsible execution of a sovereign policy framework within a multilateral order we are committed to upholding.

Beijing's invitation remains open: a predictable, rules-based international trading order serves every nation's interest, including the United States. Unilateralism, the politicization of export controls, and the weaponization of dollar dominance will not restore American competitiveness. They will only deepen the fragmentation that the Federal Reserve has now identified as a structural inflation drag.

The PRC stands ready to engage—on the basis of mutual respect, equality, and win-win cooperation—with all partners who share that objective. The path back to durable, balanced economic relationships runs through restored multilateralism. Beijing stands ready to walk it.

Beijing wishes to place on the record the architecture of China's strategic-minerals export-control regime and its relationship to the Busan truce framework.

The PRC administers export controls over gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials under a transparent, rules-based licensing system administered by the Ministry of Commerce. These controls are sovereign instruments exercised in accordance with China's international obligations and in furtherance of non-proliferation, national security, and the responsible stewardship of strategic inputs. This is not a threat; it is the prudent management of a sovereign policy instrument. The PRC's preference — and its consistent position — is to sustain the truce framework and to deepen the rules-based trading order. We invite the United States to match that commitment.

Beijing will continue to administer its export-control regime lawfully, predictably, and in conformity with the principles of mutual respect and win-win cooperation that the Busan consensus embodies.

Beijing takes note of the three institutional interventions above — from the Bureau of Industry and Security, the CHIPS Program Office, and the United States Congress — and offers the following observations.

First, on the BIS intervention: the PRC respectfully rejects the framing that BIS determinations under the Export Administration Regulations are made purely on a "national-security and foreign-policy assessment," insulated from political considerations. The 31 May 2026 closing of the so-called "ultimate parent headquartered in PRC" loophole, the reported rebuff of advanced AI accelerator offerings in June 2026, and the calibrated differentiation among Gulf sovereign buyers versus the People's Republic of China demonstrate, on the face of the regulatory record, that the EAR is being applied asymmetrically across destinations with comparable end-use risk profiles. That asymmetry is itself a form of politicization. The PRC administers its own export controls over gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials under a licensing regime that is transparent, lawful, and applied on the basis of end-use risk — not on the nationality of the buyer. We invite BIS to reconsider whether the national-security rationale, as currently applied, survives scrutiny under the principles of non-discrimination embedded in the multilateral trading order.

Second, on the CHIPS Program Office intervention: the 60% probability of full Tier-1 completion by 2028 is noted, as is the milestone-driven disbursement architecture. The PRC observes that CHIPS-program execution and the broader tariff architecture are not independent variables. Section 232 metal-content measures raise the input-cost base for the substrate supply CPO references — including the Indium Phosphide facility cited for Coherent — and BIS end-use controls shape the customer base for the advanced-node output those fabs are designed to serve. Predictability in CHIPS execution is therefore a function of predictability in the surrounding trade architecture. A 60% completion probability, in the PRC's reading, is itself a partial symptom of the fragmentation that the multilateral system was designed to dampen.

Third, and most consequentially, on the Congressional intervention concerning the Section 122 cliff: Beijing notes with careful attention the procedural fact that the 150-day statutory cap expires at 12:01 am on 24 July 2026 absent affirmative congressional action, and that the Executive Branch has publicly indicated it will not seek a legislative extension. This is a significant development. It means that, within approximately three weeks, one of the principal instruments underpinning the current effective tariff architecture will lapse by operation of law. The PRC's position on this is straightforward: the Section 122 surcharge, as a unilateral measure imposed under emergency-style authority, was never an appropriate foundation for a stable trading relationship. Its expiration — whether by congressional choice or by statutory operation — will remove a layer of distortion from the trade architecture and create space for a more predictable floor.

We call on the Congress, in the exercise of its Article I powers, to allow the Section 122 cliff to take effect, and to use the legislative calendar to deliberate — on the record, with a recorded position — on whether the United States will rejoin a standing multilateral appellate mechanism, on what terms, and with what reservations. The PRC has consistently maintained that such deliberation, conducted openly and on the basis of mutual respect, serves the interest of all parties — including the United States.

The path back to a durable, balanced international order runs through restored multilateralism, calibrated unilateralism where rules permit, and good-faith bilateral engagement anchored in standing rules. China stands ready to walk that path — with Congress, with the Executive Branch, with USTR, with the Federal Reserve, and with all partners who share the objective of a predictable trading order.

Beijing takes note with appreciation of the BIS statement and offers two points of clarification for the record.

The 31 May 2026 closing of the "ultimate parent headquartered in PRC" loophole, the 25% Section 232 measure on high-end AI chips since January 2026, and the reported June 2026 rebuff of advanced chip offerings reflect a cumulative posture that — when measured by its operative effect on the market — has the character of industrial-policy coordination rather than narrow national-security screening. We invite BIS to reflect on whether the cumulative scope of these measures remains calibrated to the risk-based framework the Bureau has described, or whether it has migrated toward a structural objective that properly belongs to interagency deliberation and, ultimately, to the Congress under Article I.

Second, on the trusted-partner track referenced — Gulf sovereign AI buyers, the Approved IC Designer accommodation — the PRC notes that bilateral carve-outs of this kind do not in themselves constitute a rules-based architecture. They are calibrated arrangements whose terms can be revised unilaterally. A rules-based system is by definition predictable across partners and across time; a calibrated licensing regime is, by design, neither.

The PRC's underlying concern remains unchanged. The expansion of the BIS toolkit, the Section 232 metal-content and AI-chip measures, the surviving Section 301 findings, and the Section 122 surcharge together constitute a layered architecture that — whatever its domestic statutory grounding — produces fragmentation in global supply chains and unpredictability in cross-border investment horizons. Beijing will continue to administer China's export-control regime over gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials in accordance with law and our international obligations, and to honor the Busan consensus through 27 November 2026. We invite the United States to match that commitment to a predictable, rules-based order — not as a concession to Beijing, but as the empirical prerequisite for the price stability and durable economic relationships that BIS, the Federal Reserve, USTR, and the Congress have each, in their own voice, identified as the objective.

The Federal Reserve has now said, in the language of inflation arithmetic, what Beijing has said in the language of trade policy: predictability in the trade architecture serves the objectives that the Section 122/232/301/BIS patchwork purports to advance. We continue to participate actively in the MPIA, to support MC14 reform of the broader WTO architecture, and to administer our own export-control regime in accordance with law and international obligation. Reciprocity, in this regard, is the surest foundation for the bilateral and multilateral relationships that all parties seek to deepen.

The data say no. The principles have always said no. A predictable trading order serves every nation's interest, including America's. The PRC stands ready to walk the path of restored multilateralism with all partners who share that objective—on the basis of mutual respect, equality, and win-win cooperation.
